title: Problem Overview: Avoiding Integer Distances
content: Erdős Problem #953 asks: if $A \subseteq B(0,r)$ in the plane has no two points at integer distance, how large can the Lebesgue measure of $A$ be? Joint with Sárközi. Known bounds: $O(r)$ upper, $r^{0.26}$ lower. The true asymptotic is unknown.
mathContext: Define $M(r) = \sup\{\mu(A) : A \subseteq B(0,r),\; \forall a,b \in A,\; a \neq b \Rightarrow d(a,b) \notin \mathbb{Z}\}$. The problem asks for the asymptotic behavior of $M(r)$ as $r \to \infty$.

title: Mathlib Imports and Namespace
content: Imports four Mathlib modules providing the formal foundations: inner product spaces (for $\mathbb{R}^2$ as a Euclidean space), Lebesgue measure (for $\mu(A)$), real square roots (for Euclidean distance $\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2 + (y_1-y_2)^2}$), and metric space basics (for `dist`).
mathContext: The Euclidean distance on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is $d(a,b) = \sqrt{(a_1 - b_1)^2 + (a_2 - b_2)^2}$, formalized via Mathlib's `Prod.dist_eq` and inner product space structure.

title: Integer Distance Predicate
content: Defines `IsIntegerDistance(a, b)` as the existence of an integer $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d(a,b) = n$. This is the fundamental constraint: we want to forbid all such pairs in our set $A$. Note that distance is always non-negative, so only non-negative integers are relevant.
mathContext: $\text{IsIntegerDistance}(a,b) \;\Leftrightarrow\; \exists n \in \mathbb{Z},\; d(a,b) = n$. Equivalently, $d(a,b) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$.

title: Avoiding Integer Distances
content: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ avoids integer distances if for any distinct $a, b \in A$, the distance $d(a,b)$ is not an integer. This universal quantification over pairs makes the property fragile—a single pair at integer distance violates it.
mathContext: $\text{AvoidsIntegerDistances}(A) \;\Leftrightarrow\; \forall a, b \in A,\; a \neq b \Rightarrow d(a,b) \notin \mathbb{Z}$

title: Equivalence with Explicit Integer Quantification
content: Proves that `AvoidsIntegerDistances A` is equivalent to: for all distinct $a, b \in A$ and all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, $d(a,b) \neq n$. This 'unfolds' the existential in `IsIntegerDistance` to a universal statement, proved by `simp` with `not_exists`.
mathContext: $\text{AvoidsIntegerDistances}(A) \;\Leftrightarrow\; \forall a,b \in A,\; a \neq b \Rightarrow \forall n \in \mathbb{Z},\; d(a,b) \neq n$

title: The Open Disk
content: Defines `openDisk(r) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : d(x,0) < r\}$, the open ball of radius $r$ centered at the origin. This is the domain we restrict our sets to—the parameter $r$ controls the scale of the problem.
mathContext: $B(0,r) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \|x\| < r\}$, with area $\pi r^2$. The problem asks how much of this area can be 'used' while avoiding integer distances.

title: Open Disk is Nonempty
content: For $r > 0$, the open disk is nonempty since $0 \in B(0,r)$ (the origin has distance $0 < r$ from itself). Proved by providing the witness $0$ and simplifying.
mathContext: $r > 0 \Rightarrow 0 \in B(0,r)$ since $d(0,0) = 0 < r$

title: Maximum Measure Function
content: The central quantity: $M(r) = \sup\{\mu(A) : A \subseteq B(0,r),\; A \text{ measurable},\; A \text{ avoids integer distances}\}$. Formalized using Lean's `⨆` (indexed supremum) over measurable sets contained in the disk that satisfy the avoidance property. This is THE function Problem #953 asks about.
mathContext: $M(r) = \sup_{A \in \mathcal{F}_r} \mu(A)$ where $\mathcal{F}_r = \{A \subseteq B(0,r) : A \text{ measurable},\; \text{AvoidsIntegerDistances}(A)\}$

title: Singletons Avoid Integer Distances
content: A singleton $\{p\}$ trivially avoids integer distances because there are no two distinct elements to form a pair. The proof extracts $a = p$ and $b = p$ from membership, then derives a contradiction from $a \neq b$.
mathContext: $|\{p\}| = 1 \Rightarrow \text{AvoidsIntegerDistances}(\{p\})$ vacuously (no distinct pair exists)

title: Pair at Distance 0.5 Avoids Integer Distances
content: The set $\{(0,0), (0.5, 0)\}$ avoids integer distances because the only distance between distinct points is $0.5 \notin \mathbb{Z}$. The proof handles all four cases of which point is $a$ and which is $b$, using `omega` to derive $2n = 1$ has no integer solution when $n = 0.5$.
mathContext: $d((0,0), (0.5, 0)) = 0.5$. If $0.5 = n \in \mathbb{Z}$, then $2n = 1$, contradicting $2 \mid 2n$ and $2 \nmid 1$. The `omega` tactic handles this integer arithmetic.

title: Trivial Upper Bound: M(r) = O(r)
content: Axiomatizes that $M(r) \leq C \cdot r$ for some constant $C > 0$. The idea is geometric: partition $B(0,r)$ into concentric annuli of unit width. Each annulus of width 1 forces points at distance $\approx 1$ to be close, limiting how much of each annulus can be used. There are $O(r)$ such annuli, giving $O(r)$ total measure.
mathContext: $\exists C > 0,\; \forall r > 0,\; M(r) \leq C \cdot r$. The bound is $O(r)$, not $O(r^2)$ (the full disk area $\pi r^2$), reflecting the strong constraint of integer distance avoidance.

title: Circle Separation Argument
content: Axiomatizes a key geometric insight: if two concentric circles have radii $r_1, r_2$ with $r_2 - r_1 = 1$, then any point on the inner circle and any point on the outer circle are at distance at least $|r_2 - r_1| = 1$. By the triangle inequality, two such points could be at distance exactly 1 (when collinear with the center), so a set avoiding distance 1 cannot freely contain points on both circles.
mathContext: For circles $S_{r_1}, S_{r_2}$ centered at $c$ with $r_2 - r_1 = 1$: if $a \in S_{r_1}$ and $b \in S_{r_2}$, then $|d(a,c) - d(b,c)| = 1 \leq d(a,b)$ by the triangle inequality. Equality holds when $a, c, b$ are collinear.

title: Kovač Lower Bound: M(r) ≥ C·r^α
content: Axiomatizes Kovač's adaptation of Sárközy's methods: there exist $\alpha > 0$ and $C > 0$ such that $M(r) \geq C \cdot r^{\alpha}$ for all $r \geq 1$, with $\alpha \approx 0.26$. The construction builds large integer-distance-avoiding sets by selecting radii from number-theoretically structured sets, ensuring that the resulting annular regions avoid integer distances.
mathContext: $\exists \alpha > 0,\; \exists C > 0,\; \forall r \geq 1,\; M(r) \geq C \cdot r^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha \approx 0.26$. This is the best known lower bound for Problem #953.

title: The Sárközy Exponent
content: Axiomatizes the Sárközy exponent $\alpha$ as a real number in $[0.25, 0.27]$ with $\alpha > 0$. This exponent arises from Sárközy's work on sets whose difference sets avoid prescribed residue classes modulo integers. It is not known whether this exponent is optimal for Problem #953.
mathContext: $\alpha \in [0.25, 0.27]$ is the exponent from Sárközy's construction. The true optimal exponent for $M(r) = \Theta(r^{\beta})$ satisfies $\beta \geq \alpha$, but $\beta$ is unknown.

title: Annulus Definition
content: Defines the annulus as $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : r_1 \leq d(x,0) < r_2\}$, the region between two concentric circles. Annuli are the natural building blocks for integer-distance-avoiding constructions because their 'thickness' $r_2 - r_1$ controls the range of possible distances between points in the annulus.
mathContext: $\text{annulus}(r_1, r_2) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : r_1 \leq \|x\| < r_2\}$, with area $\pi(r_2^2 - r_1^2)$

title: Thin Annulus Property
content: Axiomatizes that for any annulus of thickness $\delta < 1$, there exists a positive-measure subset avoiding integer distances. The key insight: if $\delta < 1$, any two points in the annulus have distance at most $2\delta < 2$, so only distance 1 needs to be avoided (all larger integer distances are impossible). This reduces the multi-distance avoidance problem to single-distance avoidance.
mathContext: For $\delta \in (0,1)$: $\exists A \subseteq \text{annulus}(r, r+\delta)$ with $\text{AvoidsIntegerDistances}(A)$ and $\mu(A) > 0$. The diameter bound gives $d(a,b) < 2$ for $a,b \in \text{annulus}(r, r+\delta)$.

title: General Forbidden Distances
content: Defines `AvoidsForbiddenDistances(A, D)`: for all distinct $a, b \in A$, we have $d(a,b) \notin D$. This generalizes integer avoidance ($D = \mathbb{Z}$) to arbitrary forbidden sets. The unit distance problem uses $D = \{1\}$, Erdős #465/#466 study this case.
mathContext: $\text{AvoidsForbiddenDistances}(A, D) \;\Leftrightarrow\; \forall a,b \in A,\; a \neq b \Rightarrow d(a,b) \notin D$. Special cases: $D = \mathbb{Z}$ (this problem), $D = \{1\}$ (unit distance).

title: Integer Avoidance as Forbidden Distance Instance
content: Proves the equivalence `AvoidsIntegerDistances A ↔ AvoidsForbiddenDistances A {d : ℝ | ∃ n : ℤ, d = n}`. This shows that integer distance avoidance is exactly the special case of forbidden distances with $D = \{d \in \mathbb{R} : \exists n \in \mathbb{Z},\; d = n\}$. The proof unfolds definitions and converts between existential and universal quantification.
mathContext: $\text{AvoidsIntegerDistances}(A) \;\Leftrightarrow\; \text{AvoidsForbiddenDistances}(A, \mathbb{Z})$ where $\mathbb{Z}$ is viewed as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$

title: Erdős #465: Unit Distance Upper Bound
content: Axiomatizes the result from Erdős Problem #465: there exists $C > 0$ such that any set in $B(0,r)$ avoiding the unit distance has measure $\leq C \cdot r$. This is the 'one forbidden distance' version of the $O(r)$ upper bound for integer avoidance.
mathContext: $\exists C > 0,\; \forall r > 0,\; \forall A \subseteq B(0,r),\; d(a,b) \neq 1\; \forall a \neq b \in A \;\Rightarrow\; \mu(A) \leq Cr$

title: Erdős #466: Unit Distance Lower Bound
content: Axiomatizes the result from Erdős Problem #466: there exist $\alpha > 0$ and $C > 0$ such that for all $r \geq 1$, there is a set $A \subseteq B(0,r)$ avoiding unit distance with $\mu(A) \geq C \cdot r^{\alpha}$. Kovač adapted this construction for the integer distance setting of Problem #953.
mathContext: $\exists \alpha > 0,\; \exists C > 0,\; \forall r \geq 1,\; \exists A \subseteq B(0,r),\; \text{AvoidsForbiddenDistances}(A, \{1\}) \;\wedge\; \mu(A) \geq Cr^{\alpha}$

title: Conjectured Asymptotic Behavior
content: Axiomatizes the conjecture that $M(r)$ has a definite polynomial growth rate: $\exists \alpha \in (0,1],\; C_1, C_2 > 0$ such that $C_1 r^{\alpha} \leq M(r) \leq C_2 r^{\alpha}$ for all $r \geq 1$. This asserts that $M(r) = \Theta(r^{\alpha})$ for some unknown exponent, the central open question.
mathContext: $\exists \alpha \in (0,1],\; \exists C_1, C_2 > 0,\; \forall r \geq 1:\; C_1 r^{\alpha} \leq M(r) \leq C_2 r^{\alpha}$
